gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1011r:
Environmental Cleanup, GAO-05-1011R of September 16, 2005, takes up who must pay to clean up perchlorate, a rocket fuel part that taints water and soil. The chemical has turned up in 35 states, the District of Columbia, and 2 commonwealths. It harms the thyroid gland. Care centers on a plant site in Henderson, Nevada, where the Navy and private firms made the chemical for decades.

Congress asked who bears the cost, the blame, and the duty to pay at such sites. The letter walks through the site's owners and the cleanup now under way. It frames the legal fight over bills for a mess with mixed public and private roots.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1021r:
Overview of the Long-Term Care Partnership Program, GAO-05-1021R of September 9, 2005, explains a state plan to shift long-term care costs off Medicaid. Care costs hit $183 billion in 2003. Medicaid paid nearly half. Private insurance paid about $16 billion, or 9 percent. Costs were set to climb fast as the baby boom group aged.

Under the plan, states bless some private care policies. Buyers use policy payouts first if they later need care. They may then keep some assets and still qualify for Medicaid aid. Congress asked for this plain summary of how the trade-off works and who it draws in.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-311r:
Veterans Affairs Homeless Programs, GAO-05-311R of March 16, 2005, asks why a housing plan for homeless veterans has built nothing in 6 years. A 1998 law let the agency back loans to build or fix blocks of short-stay homes for veterans with no roof. Such homes would aid cure from drink and drugs. They would help men and women rebuild work and kin ties.

No block stands open yet. GAO lists what the agency has done to launch the plan since the law passed. It names the snags that kept each step slow, from loan terms to site rules. The gap sits between a kind law and a stalled start.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-481r:
The twelfth report on Haitian immigration cases required by law is GAO-05-481R, a letter dated April 14, 2005. The Haitian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act of 1998 let some Haitian nationals and their families apply to become legal permanent residents. The act orders the Comptroller General to report every 6 months on how many applied and how many were approved. Reports must continue until every case is finally decided.

Through February 28, 2005, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had received 39,050 applications under the act. It had approved 13,045 of them. The Executive Office for Immigration Review had 1,635 applications filed and had approved 568. The letter breaks the totals down by class of applicant. Classes include asylum seekers, parolees, children without parents, and orphaned or abandoned children. Eligible spouses, children, and unmarried sons and daughters are counted as dependents. The letter is a short status record in a long series.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-501r:
For the 82nd Airborne Division Association, GAO's review of outside audit reports is set out in GAO-05-501R, a letter of June 10, 2005. The association builds fellowship among current and former troopers across the United States. Two fiscal years are covered here: those ended December 31, 2003, and December 31, 2002.

Like every federally chartered corporation, the association must publish yearly statements of what it owns, owes, earns, and spends. An independent accountant must audit them. GAO read the financial statements and the auditor's reports and ran analytical checks on the data. It also spoke briefly with the group's auditor about ways its reporting could be improved. No failure to meet the legal reporting duties was found. The auditor concluded that the statements were fairly stated under standard accounting rules. GAO notes that its read was not an audit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-511r:
For the Military Order of the World Wars, GAO's letter is GAO-05-511R, issued June 10, 2005. The order promotes ties among those who served as officers. It also backs patriotic education and the study of military, naval, and air science. Its audit report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2003, is the subject here.

Three duties in the charter statute frame the review. The order must file yearly financial statements in fair detail. It must obtain an audit by an independent public accountant. It must submit the report and statements to Congress. GAO read the statements and the auditor's report and made limited checks of the figures. It found no instance of noncompliance to report. The auditor's opinion used a modified cash basis of accounting and held the statements fairly presented on that basis. GAO rendered no audit opinion of its own.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-581r:
Drug prices that hospitals actually pay are gathered for rate setters in a GAO letter, GAO-05-581R, dated June 30, 2005. Medicare pays hospitals set rates for outpatient care, drugs included, under its outpatient payment system. Those rates rest on hospital costs from 1996. New drugs for cancer, rare blood disorders, and other grave illness raised a worry. Hospitals might shun costly new products if payments lagged their prices, and patients could lose access.

Congress answered in 1999 with temporary pass-through payments to top up the rates for new products. Sound rates still need sound price data. The letter gives the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services the purchase prices GAO collected for its use in setting outpatient rates.  Readers get the price evidence behind the payment debate, rather than a broad program review. The letter sits within a long argument over how Medicare should pay for new drug therapies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-591r:
NASA's fiscal year 2004 management representation letter is the topic of GAO report GAO-05-591R, issued on June 23, 2005. The agency's letter helps support the audit of the government's consolidated financial statements. GAO checked the letter in five key areas set by the federal audit manual. Improvements were needed in two areas, and both were narrow.

First, the agency gave no materiality thresholds. Those figures show which matters NASA treated as large enough to count. The Treasury and the budget office rely on agency thresholds when they frame the government-wide letter. Second, the letter carried 25 of the 28 standard representations that applied to NASA. The other 3 were present but not in full. GAO made two recommendations to the agency's chief financial officer. It also asked the inspector general, with the outside audit firm, to help bring future letters up to the mark. NASA officials commented on the draft.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-601r:
A disagreement marks the representation letter review for the U.S. Agency for International Development: GAO-05-601R, dated July 22, 2005. The letter covers fiscal year 2004 and supports the audit of the government's financial statements. GAO checked five key areas and found fault in just one. The agency's own leaders, though, disputed even that finding.

The fault lay in the summary of uncorrected misstatements sent with the letter. The summary did not name the ledger accounts or statement lines the errors touched. It also gave no description of the misstatements themselves. GAO recommended that the chief financial officer include a complete summary in future letters, with descriptions. It asked the acting inspector general to help the agency meet that condition. In separate comments, the finance chief and the acting inspector general disagreed with GAO's conclusion. Their dispute makes this the contested entry in an otherwise routine series.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-641r:
Written answers to senators' follow-up questions make up GAO letter GAO-05-641R of April 29, 2005. The topic is the defense department's planned National Security Personnel System, a pay-for-performance scheme for civilian staff. Most answers return to one theme: change this large fails without the workforce. Staff and their unions must be brought in early, kept in, and heard in ways that change outcomes, not just fill a box.

GAO urges top appointees to lead talks themselves and to track morale through surveys and hotlines. Lawsuits by unions at two departments show the cost of weak buy-in. Leadership that listens but never adjusts, GAO warns, breeds exits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-691r:
Recommendations on the securities agency's own books fill GAO letter GAO-05-691R of July 27, 2005. GAO's audit of the agency's fiscal 2004 statements found material weaknesses in three areas. Two are covered here: how fines and disgorgements from law-breakers are recorded, and how the statements themselves are built. Eighteen recommendations target those flaws. The third area, computer security, drew six recommendations in a March 2005 report.

The letter is the detailed half of the audit's advice. It leaves the agency a checklist for fixing how it counts the money it seizes and reports its own finances.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-771r:
More written answers on the same personnel system appear in GAO-05-771R, a letter from June 14, 2005. The Comptroller General had testified on April 12, 2005. The hearing was titled around reaching readiness for the new system. Lawmakers asked GAO to answer further questions for the record. Those questions covered the major areas of concern.

The letter gives GAO's replies in full. They address how the Defense Department plans to design and launch the system for its civilian workforce. Readers get the concerns in one place, with GAO's view on each. The piece adds detail to the public record built by the spring hearings on the system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-791r:
A tiny federal commission gets an audit in GAO-05-791R, a report from July 21, 2005. The body promotes acts of remembrance for those who died in service. Congress gave it $1 million for fiscal years 2002 through 2004. The law tells GAO to audit its money dealings. This report covers fiscal year 2004.

GAO found most dealings were backed and approved. Still, it found many chances to tighten control. Pay of about $135,000 lacked signed time sheets. The body's records differed from the veterans agency that processes its funds by about $59,000. The two settled the gap in May 2005. Buying and travel rules were not always followed. GAO linked many faults to the body's small size.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-941r:
Written answers on judiciary space costs make up GAO-05-941R, a letter dated July 27, 2005. GAO had testified on June 21, 2005, at an oversight hearing. The hearing covered the judiciary's ability to pay for current and future space. Congress sent added questions on June 23, 2005. They concern the buildings fund and how judges manage space needs.

GAO answered mainly from its past work and knowledge in the area. It did not seek agency comments on a draft. That is because the reply rests on products already issued, the letter notes. Readers get the fund's mechanics and the judiciary's space steps in answer form. The letter completes the hearing record on a topic GAO had tracked for years: courthouse costs and rent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-991r:
Pension insurer practices on likely claims are answered in GAO-05-991R, a letter dated September 9, 2005. The single-employer program insures over 34 million people in over 29,000 plans. GAO placed it on the high-risk list in 2003. The program swung from a $9.7 billion surplus in fiscal year 2000 to a $23.3 billion deficit by September 2004.

Most of that deficit, 73 percent or $16.9 billion, rests on probable claims. Those are plans the insurer deems likely to end. Over 95 percent of such plans have in fact ended over time, GAO notes. The letter answers questions about how the insurer treats these likely claims. Readers can see the method behind the biggest slice of the deficit. The piece adds to GAO's long record of warnings on the program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1051r:
Posthearing answers on Secure Flight make up GAO-06-1051R, a letter dated August 4, 2006. Congress held a hearing on June 14, 2006, on the security agency's intelligence office. The hearing covered progress and challenges in the passenger prescreening program. At it, GAO noted that for over 3 years the agency had faced many challenges in building the program. A core cause was the lack of a disciplined life cycle approach.

This letter answers the follow-up questions Congress sent. It adds detail on the program's development and the agency's handling of it. Readers can pair the letter with the hearing statement for the full record. The exchange shows the questions lawmakers still pressed after the hearing. It keeps the troubled program's oversight trail complete in public form.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-151r:
The cost of federal water rules for towns and cities is probed in GAO-06-151R, a letter report dated November 30, 2005. Two laws, the Safe Drinking Water Act and the Clean Water Act, set national water standards. Local systems must meet them: about 53,000 drinking water systems, 17,000 wastewater plants, and 7,000 storm sewer systems. Meeting the rules can mean new treatment gear and higher bills. Towns voice growing worry about the total burden, above all from newer rules.

The letter studies why the cost impact is so hard to pin down. The aid agency, water groups, and others have built cost estimates over the years. Their methods and scope differ, so totals clash. Local factors, from plant age to growth, swing the price widely. GAO lays out the traps in forecasting such costs. The letter helps Congress weigh clean water gains against the strain on local budgets.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-301r:
Cost accounting practice in three big departments is surveyed in GAO-06-301R, a letter dated December 19, 2005. Laws and standards have long pressed agencies to track what their work costs. The 1990 finance law asks agency finance chiefs to build systems that report costs. Federal standards spell out how costs should be assigned to goals and outputs. GAO reviewed the Education, Transportation, and Treasury departments.

GAO made 17 recommendations to the three secretaries. Education's finance chief should issue a department-wide policy, the letter urges. Staff should watch how units carry it out and keep controls sound. Reliable cost data let managers price programs honestly and spot waste. Without them, budgets rest on habit rather than evidence. The three departments differ in size and mission, which tests the standards' reach. The letter treats cost accounting as plumbing: unseen, vital, and often neglected until it leaks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-321r:
The crew who will run the Capitol's new cooling plant is the concern of GAO-06-321R, a letter dated February 10, 2006. The West Refrigeration Plant expansion anchors a push to grow the Capitol Power Plant's capacity. Some of its gear dates to the 1950s. The new plant will lift chilled water output by about 23 percent. The total project budget stands at $100.9 million. Work was set to finish in March 2006, with changes possibly pushing it to June.

New machines need trained people, and staffing is the letter's warning. The Architect of the Capitol must commission the plant and run it safely. Thin staffing or thin training could waste the investment or court accidents. The letter ties a construction story to an operations one. Buildings get the headlines; the crews who keep them cool decide whether the money worked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-41r:
The Olympic committee's books for three years pass GAO's review. Letter GAO-06-41R, dated October 7, 2005, covers the United States Olympic Committee. The audit reports run for fiscal years ended December 31, 2001, through 2003. The committee's purpose is to set national goals for amateur sports. It also aids and encourages reaching those goals.

Federal law requires chartered corporations to file yearly financial statements. An independent public accountant must audit them. GAO read the statements, notes, and auditor's reports. It spoke with the committee's chief financial officer. GAO found no reportable instance of noncompliance. The auditors said the statements were presented fairly under U.S. accounting rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-461r:
Emergency contracts after two hurricanes are the subject of this briefing record. Letter report GAO-06-461R, dated March 15, 2006, covers agency management of contractors after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita. GAO briefed Congress on the review in February 2006. Three agencies sit at the center. They are the Federal Emergency Management Agency, the Army Corps of Engineers, and the General Services Administration.

GAO assessed how each agency planned for key response contracts. It also judged how each oversaw those contracts during recovery work. The review was done under the Comptroller General's legal authority. Readers get a cross-agency view of contract planning and control. The record is a briefing summary, so detail is compact.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-61r:
Building costs at the Securities and Exchange Commission are the subject of GAO-06-61R, a briefing report dated October 20, 2005. In May 2005, the SEC told Congress it had found about $48 million in costs it had not budgeted. The costs came from building new facilities in Washington, D.C., and fixing up leased space in New York City and Boston. The SEC asked to shift funds from 2005 and 2006 to cover the gap.

GAO broke down how much of the cost was unplanned and why estimates missed the mark. The added costs were $20.2 million for 2005 and $28.5 million for 2006. GAO also reviewed steps the SEC took once the problem surfaced. The report shows how weak cost estimates can strain an agency budget.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-651r:
A small Senate fund is the subject of GAO-06-651R, a GAO letter report dated June 27, 2006. The Senate Office of Public Records Revolving Fund handles money tied to public records work, such as lobby disclosure filings. At the request of the Secretary of the Senate, GAO performed agreed-upon procedures on the fund. The work covered fiscal years 2003 through 2005. GAO checked receipt and payment processing and related steps.

GAO inspected documents that backed the fund's receipts and payments. GAO also reviewed how the office and the Senate Disbursing Office reconciled their records. The work followed government auditing standards and attestation standards for such agreed procedures. The report gives Senate managers a factual record of what the checks found, without a broader audit opinion.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-671r:
Federal wildfire strategy gets a status check in GAO-06-671R, a letter report dated May 1, 2006. Wildfire was a growing national problem. Acres burned each year from 2000 to 2005 ran 70 percent above the 1990s average. Federal wildfire funding nearly tripled, from about $1 billion in fiscal year 1999 to nearly $3 billion a few years later. GAO had urged agencies to build one cohesive strategy for the threat.

GAO reported that agencies still had not prepared a tactical plan with steps and time frames for finishing that strategy. A February 2006 interagency paper on fuels treatment was a step forward. But it did not set out long-term options or the funding they would need. GAO pressed the agencies to complete the plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-691r:
Fallen firefighters are honored by the group whose audit GAO reviewed in GAO-06-691R, a letter report dated May 12, 2006. The National Fallen Firefighters Foundation holds a federal charter. It honors firefighters who die in the line of duty and runs the national memorial service for them. It also aids their families and promotes public fire safety awareness. Its statements for fiscal years 2003 and 2002 were audited by an outside accountant.

GAO examined the audit reports on those statements. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance with the law's reporting rules. The auditor's opinion said the statements were presented fairly under United States accounting principles. GAO's letter records the finding for Congress. The check confirms the foundation met its yearly reporting duty.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-731r:
Game and fish restoration funds are the subject of GAO-06-731R, a letter report dated July 5, 2006. The Fish and Wildlife Service runs federal aid programs that send hunting and fishing fees back to states for wildlife work. In 1999 and 2000, GAO testified that the service managed and oversaw those funds poorly. GAO described instances of funds used in ways that broke program rules. This letter updates the corrective actions taken since then.

GAO reported that the program was making progress on the concerns raised earlier. The letter builds on an April 2006 briefing GAO gave to the subcommittee. It details problems found and the fixes the service put in place. A funding history for the two programs is included. The update shows oversight slowly catching up with a troubled program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-741r:
New border document rules are observed in GAO-06-741R, a letter report dated May 25, 2006. For years, United States and Canadian citizens crossed the northern border with a driver's license or birth certificate. Some crossed with no documents at all. In 2005, an estimated 13 million United States citizens crossed from Canada. The Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative would require passports or approved cards by a statutory deadline of January 2008.

GAO reported on efforts to put the initiative in place on the Canadian border. GAO asked whether the deadline could be met. GAO also set out challenges tied to substitute documents and programs, such as the proposed PASS card. Cost, enrollment, and border delays all drew concern. The letter captures an early test of post-9/11 border policy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-751r:
Promotion and enforcement data from two border agencies fill GAO-06-751R, a letter report dated June 13, 2006. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection were both formed inside the Homeland Security Department in March 2003. They grew out of the former Immigration and Naturalization Service and the Customs Service. Merging 22 agencies into one department reshaped their missions and staffs. Congress asked GAO for facts on enforcement work and on who wins supervisory promotions.

The letter presents information on immigration enforcement activity by the two agencies. It also reports data on supervisory promotions, broken out for review by lawmakers. GAO presents the figures as an information record rather than a broad audit. Readers can trace how the young agencies staffed their leadership ranks in their first years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-791r:
A Commerce Department buying vehicle is examined in GAO-06-791R, a letter report dated June 14, 2006. The contract, called Commerce Information Technology Solutions Next Generation, lets agencies buy technology services governmentwide. Concerns had been raised about its bid down approach, in which firms cut prices through rounds of bidding. Critics questioned whether that method is fair to vendors. A fiscal year 2006 funding report asked GAO to review the contract.

The letter transmits the results of GAO's review to the committees that asked for it. It weighs how the bid down approach worked and how it treated competing firms. Governmentwide contracts shape billions in buying, so their rules matter. Readers can follow GAO's account of the process and its fairness questions. The review adds a check on a widely used contract.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-921r:
Audit results for the National Fallen Firefighters Foundation are relayed in GAO letter GAO-06-921R, dated July 7, 2006. The foundation honors firefighters who die on duty, runs the national memorial service, and aids their families. As a federally chartered group, it must file audited yearly statements.

GAO read the outside audit reports for the fiscal years that ended December 31, 2004 and 2003. The auditors held that the statements were fairly shown under U.S. accounting rules. GAO found no case of rule breaking that had to be reported. The short letter gives Congress that clean audit result, in the form the charter law requires.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1171r:
Classical plant and animal breeding at the farm department is inventoried in GAO letter GAO-07-1171R, dated September 13, 2007. Classical breeding mates and selects stock for good traits, without adding genes from other species. Two research arms lead that work at the Department of Agriculture. One runs over 100 labs, with about $1.3 billion in fiscal year 2006 funds.

Congress found such breeding hard to price as a public cost. GAO was asked what staff and funds go to it. It was asked the same of gene-based breeding work. It listed outside breeding projects the department funds. The letter gives Congress a first full count of a quiet, vital craft.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1201r:
Prescription drug prices rose faster than inflation in the early 2000s. In GAO-07-1201R, dated September 7, 2007, GAO updated its tracking of retail drug prices. The study covered drugs used often by Medicare enrollees and by people with other health coverage. Prices came from two state pharmacy assistance programs. The measure used was the usual and customary price for a 30-day supply.

GAO found that average monthly prices rose 13.6 percent from January 2004 through January 2007. That gain covered 122 frequently used drugs, a pace of 4.3 percent per year. Prices rose at similar rates for drugs used by each enrollee group. Brand-name drug prices went up over the three years. Prices for the 57 generic drugs in the set fell instead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1261r:
America's long-term budget path points toward debt that grows faster than the economy. GAO updated its outlook in GAO-07-1261R, a letter dated September 28, 2007. Since 1992, GAO has run long-term fiscal simulations under varied policy paths. This update used the Congressional Budget Office's August projections. It also drew on new Social Security and Medicare trustee reports. GAO pairs the federal view with its study of state and local budgets.

The letter's finding is blunt: federal fiscal policy remains unsustainable. That held despite recent improvement in the annual deficit. The simulations show strain building over time under current paths. GAO stressed that federal, state, and local fiscal problems are linked. It urged leaders to weigh them together in a strategic way. Readers get the August 2007 snapshot of a warning GAO refreshes three times a year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-131r:
Highway projects draw on fuel and other excise taxes held in a trust fund. In GAO-07-131R, dated November 3, 2006, GAO reports agreed-upon procedures on that fund's tax revenue. The work aided the Transportation Department's inspector general. It covers the fiscal year ended September 30, 2006. The question was whether net excise tax revenue sent to the Highway Trust Fund was supported by the records.

The agreed procedures ranged across eight areas of the tax pipeline. They tested sample transactions and the tax agency's quarterly certifications to the fund. They checked Treasury adjustments and estimates for the fourth quarter of the year. They also reconciled tax records against Treasury records. GAO states plainly that judging whether the procedures were adequate is the department's job. The enclosure sets out each procedure with the findings it produced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-291r:
Freight rail rates jumped in 2005 by the most in two decades. GAO updated its rail study in GAO-07-291R, a letter dated August 15, 2007. Congress deregulated the industry in 1980. Shippers with no rival carrier can challenge rates past a cost threshold. GAO's October 2006 report traced rates through 2004. This letter adds the 2005 data. It covers rates, side charges, and possibly captive traffic.

Industry rates rose 7 percent in 2005, GAO reports. Inflation ran 5 percent that year. Rates beat inflation for only the second time in 20 years. They still sit below 1985 levels. Coal and grain rates rose too. Side revenue, which includes fuel surcharges, nearly tripled. It climbed from $633 million in 2004 to $1.7 billion in 2005. Traffic possibly captive to one railroad kept falling. But traffic priced far above the relief threshold grew.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-381r:
Urban terror grants grew tenfold in two years, then shrank, and the formula changed midstream. GAO explained the process in GAO-07-381R, a letter dated February 7, 2007. The letter shares a November 17, 2006 briefing to Congress. Urban grants reached $830 million in fiscal year 2005 across 43 areas. In fiscal year 2006 they fell to about $711 million. Eligible areas dropped to 35. GAO studied the new risk method. It also studied how planned spending was judged.

The department rebuilt its risk scoring for 2006, GAO reports. It added a review of how well grant plans would work. Scores from both reviews set the awards. For fiscal year 2007, 69 kinds of data feed the risk model. Of those, 38 come from a single source each. One asset data supplier had failed GAO's reliability checks before. Lawmakers questioned the method's fairness. The briefing laid out the planned 2007 changes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-471r: The citizenship conference's ledgers got checked in 2007, and GAO's letter audits the National Conference on Citizenship's finances in full detail. The findings deliver the formal opinion for the record. The letter proves the civic groups face the same ledger rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-571r: The device-makers' fee money got a look in 2007 — GAO's letter reports revenue data on the firms in the medical-device user-fee program. The findings lay out the numbers in full. The letter keeps the fee-for-review deal transparent for the public.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-61r: The memorial commission's money got a GAO look in 2007, and the letter goes over the audit of its books. The findings give the technical verdict. The letter shows even the tribute-builders got checked. The commemoration's cash got its audit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-621r: Selling Social Security reform cost real money in 2007 — GAO's letter tallies the administration's promotional spending. The findings put a price tag on the persuasion campaign for private accounts. Whatever one's view of the plan, the letter insists the sales job itself be counted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-771r: One fee system for truckers inched ahead in 2007 — GAO's letter says the unified carrier registry made progress but still faced headwinds. The findings track the rollout's fits and starts. The letter's theme: one nation, one truck-fee system, and a long road of headaches.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-871r: Books that talk changed blind lives — and GAO's 2007 letter looks at the talking-books program for the blind. The findings review the free audio library service. The letter celebrates a quiet marvel: the nation's bookshelf, spoken aloud for those who cannot see it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-891r: Trouble at 30,000 feet got a steadier response by 2007 — GAO's letter says federal coordination for in-flight threats had grown up, though procedures still needed polish. The findings credit the post-9/11 drill work while flagging the rough edges. Safer skies, the letter says, still had homework.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-941r: Military moms' birth care got a price check in 2007 — GAO's letter reviews TRICARE's new pay rules for civilian obstetricians. The findings track how the changes affected access and rates. Behind the policy prose sits a simple test: could service families still get a good doctor for the big day?
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-101r: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report revealing that some recipients of Hurricane Katrina and Rita disaster assistance also had unpaid federal taxes. The findings show aid dollars flowing to people who were delinquent on their own tax obligations, raising questions about screening at the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The report examines how many such cases existed and what controls could prevent repeat payments.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1041r: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at commercial Aviation: Impact of Airline Crew Scheduling on Delays and Cancellations of Commercial Flights. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-121r: GAO wrote Congress in 2007 about the Pentagon's bet on one big supply shop: shifting stock, store, and ship duties from the armed services to a single logistics agency. The letter checks whether the merger saved cash and ran smooth. The findings test a classic centralize-or-not gamble — with the military's pantry on the line.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-181r: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on VA and DOD Health Care: Administration of DOD's Post-Deployment Health Reassessment to National Guard and Reserve Servicemembers and VA's Interaction with DOD. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-201r: In 2007, the Government Accountability Office published this report on agreed-Upon Procedures: Senate Office of Public Records Revolving Fund, Fiscal Years 2006 and 2007. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-331r: In 2007, the Government Accountability Office published this report on defense Acquisitions: Status of the Expeditionary Fire Support System. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-421r: The Government Accountability Office dug into transportation Safety: Medical Certification and Background Check Requirements for Pilots, Vessel Masters, and Commercial Drivers Vary in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
